description: Part I of the Indian Constitution deals with the Union and its Territories, while Part II contains provisions related to Citizenship. India follows the concept of Single Citizenship, inspired by the British Constitution.

sections.title: The Union and its Territory
sections.description: Articles 1 to 4 under Part I of the Constitution describe the Indian Union and its territorial extent.

polity_articles.provision: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
polity_articles.details: It defines the nature of the Indian Union and clarifies that states have no right to secede from the federation.

polity_articles.provision: Grants Parliament the power to admit or establish new States.
polity_articles.details: This applies to territories that are not already part of the Indian Union (Example: Admission of Sikkim).

polity_articles.provision: Parliament can form new States and alter the areas, boundaries, or names of existing States.
polity_articles.details: The views of the concerned State Legislature are taken, but they are not binding on the Parliament.

important_facts.fact: The names of the States and Union Territories, along with their territorial extent, are listed in the First Schedule of the Constitution.

sections.title: Reorganization of States and Union Territories
sections.description: The historical process of reorganizing states on a linguistic basis and the administration of Union Territories.

key_concepts.explanation: Both committees rejected the linguistic basis for the reorganization of states and instead prioritized administrative convenience.
Broadly accepted language as the basis for reorganization of states but rejected the theory of 'one language-one state'.

historical_events.significance: It became the first linguistic state in India, created by separating the Telugu-speaking areas from the Madras State.
Enacted alongside the 7th Constitutional Amendment, it reorganized the country into 14 States and 6 Union Territories.
Bifurcated the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir into two separate Union Territories: Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

polity_articles.provision: Every Union Territory shall be administered by the President acting through an Administrator (or Lt. Governor).
polity_articles.details: Covered under Part VIII of the Constitution.

polity_articles.provision: Special provisions with respect to Delhi.
polity_articles.details: Inserted by the 69th Amendment Act, 1991, which designated Delhi as the 'National Capital Territory' (NCT).

sections.title: Citizenship: Constitutional Provisions
sections.description: Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5 to 11) deals with the citizenship of individuals at the commencement of the Constitution.

key_concepts.explanation: Despite having a federal structure, India provides for only a single citizenship for the entire country, a feature borrowed from the British Constitution.

polity_articles.provision: Deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950).
polity_articles.details: Grants citizenship based on domicile, migration from Pakistan, and registration of Indians living abroad.

polity_articles.provision: Persons voluntarily acquiring the citizenship of a foreign State shall not remain citizens of India.
polity_articles.details: This article strictly enforces the principle of Single Citizenship.

polity_articles.provision: Empowers the Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.
polity_articles.details: Using this power, the Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act of 1955.

sections.title: Citizenship Act, 1955
sections.description: The primary legislation that governs the acquisition and loss of Indian citizenship after the commencement of the Constitution.

key_concepts.explanation: Citizenship can be acquired by: 1. Birth, 2. Descent, 3. Registration, 4. Naturalization, and 5. Incorporation of Territory.

Citizenship can be lost by: 1. Renunciation (voluntarily giving it up), 2. Termination (automatically lost upon acquiring another country's citizenship), and 3. Deprivation (compulsory cancellation by the government for fraud or disloyalty).

historical_events.significance: Provided a pathway to Indian citizenship for persecuted religious minorities (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians) from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who entered India on or before December 31, 2014.

sections.title: Overseas Indians: NRI, PIO, and OCI
sections.description: Important terms and concepts related to Indians living abroad and persons of Indian origin.

key_associations.extra_info: An Indian citizen who holds an Indian passport but resides abroad for employment, business, or education. They retain their right to vote in Indian elections.
A foreign citizen of Indian origin. They are granted a lifelong visa-free entry to India but do not have voting rights or the right to hold constitutional posts.
Celebrated to mark the contribution of the overseas Indian community to the development of India, commemorating Mahatma Gandhi's return from South Africa in 1915.
